questions.question: How would you design a multi-step React form without losing user data?
questions.title: Designing a Resilient Multi-Step React Form
questions.direct_answer: Keep one draft above the individual step screens, give each step a stable URL, and update only its part of the draft. Validate before moving forward and validate the whole payload on final submit. If refresh recovery is required, persist non-sensitive draft data to session storage or a server draft, then clear it after successful completion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether route position, draft ownership, validation, and recovery are separated.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Keeping values inside unmounted steps or persisting sensitive data automatically.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define direct-entry behavior, storage policy, and final server validation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: One parent draft owns values shared by every step.
Stable step URLs make Back, Forward, and deep links predictable.
Validate the current step before advancing; validate everything at final submit.
Persist only when refresh recovery is required, with a clear expiry and privacy policy.
The server revalidates and protects the final write from accidental duplicates.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I would separate the draft data from the currently visible step. A parent component, form provider, route layout, or server draft owns the complete values, while each step reads and updates only the fields it displays. Moving between child screens then does not destroy the draft when one step unmounts.

Each step should have a stable URL such as `/apply/profile` and `/apply/contact`. That makes browser Back and Forward useful and lets the application restore the correct screen. Before moving forward, the current step validates its required fields; going backward normally keeps the existing draft without blocking the user.

For example, a job application can keep name and email in one draft while profile and contact routes edit them separately. A progress indicator derives from the route, not from a second unrelated step counter, so the URL and visible state cannot drift apart.

In-memory state survives route changes but not a document refresh. If recovery is a requirement, non-sensitive values can be saved to `sessionStorage` with guarded parsing, or the backend can own a draft for cross-device recovery. Sensitive data, expiry, schema changes, and shared-device privacy must shape that decision.

Final submission validates the complete draft again on both client and server. Pending and error states prevent silent loss, and successful completion clears the saved draft. This gives each concern one owner: route for position, draft for data, and server for the final trusted record.

sections.title: Position and data are different pieces of state
sections.content: The route answers ‘which step is visible?’ while the draft answers ‘what has the learner entered?’ Keeping them separate prevents an unmounted step from taking its values with it. Persistence is a product requirement, not an automatic choice, because saving form data creates privacy and versioning responsibilities.

sections.title: Define ownership, transition guards, and recovery before building steps
sections.content:
Place the shared draft at the nearest stable ancestor of all step routes. A form context can reduce prop passing, but it does not change ownership. Each field still needs a defined initial value, and each step should update the same draft rather than cloning a private version that later needs merging.

Treat Next as a guarded transition. Validate the visible step, focus the first error, and navigate only after it passes. Back should preserve data and rarely demand validation. Directly opening a later step needs an explicit rule: allow partial completion, redirect to the first incomplete step, or load a server draft. The application should not guess silently.

Refresh recovery can use session storage for short-lived, same-tab drafts or a backend identifier for durable and cross-device drafts. Parse stored JSON defensively and version complex drafts so deployments can migrate or discard incompatible data. Never persist passwords, payment secrets, or other sensitive fields merely for convenience.

At completion, assemble one payload, revalidate cross-step rules, disable repeat submission, and let the server enforce the authoritative rules. Clear local persistence only after a confirmed success so a temporary failure does not erase the person’s work.

sections.title: Route chooses the step while one draft survives every transition
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[stable wizard owner] --> B[shared draft]
  A --> C[current route]
  C --> D[profile step]
  C --> E[contact step]
  D -->|update profile fields| B
  E -->|update contact fields| B
  D -->|valid Next| E
  E -->|Back| D
  B --> F[optional session or server draft]
  B --> G[final full validation]
  G --> H[server validates and saves]
```

sections.title: Keep a route-based wizard draft and recover it after refresh

questions.question: How should a React app handle deep links and invalid dynamic route IDs?
questions.title: Deep Links and Invalid Route Parameters
questions.direct_answer: Treat the URL parameter as untrusted input. A deep link should load the required resource independently, display a pending state, and distinguish not found, forbidden, and failed requests. Validate the parameter before using it, cancel stale requests when the URL changes, and render intentional route-level recovery instead of assuming navigation always started inside the app.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether a dynamic route can load independently and handle every outcome.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trusting URL text or depending on state from the previous list screen.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish malformed, missing, forbidden, failed, and stale-request states.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A deep-linked screen must work without prior in-app navigation state.
Parse and validate route parameters before treating them as domain IDs.
Represent loading, success, not found, forbidden, and failure separately.
Abort or ignore stale requests when the parameter changes.
Use links with real URLs so a resource view can be copied and restored.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A deep link is a URL that opens a specific application state directly, such as `/projects/atlas`. The page cannot depend on a previous list screen having placed the project in component state. It must be able to read the route parameter, load or select the resource, and build the screen from that information alone.

I treat the parameter as untrusted URL text. A numeric ID must be parsed and range-checked; a slug must meet the expected format. After validation, the data layer loads the resource and the UI represents pending, success, not found, forbidden, and unexpected failure as different states.

For example, opening `/projects/missing` should show a clear project-not-found screen with a link back to the project list. It should not throw because a lookup returned `undefined`, and it should not disguise an authorization failure as a successful empty page unless the product deliberately avoids revealing existence.

When navigation changes the ID quickly, the earlier request may finish later and overwrite the new screen. An abort signal, router loader cancellation, or request identity check prevents that stale result. The backend still validates authorization for every resource request.

A dependable dynamic route therefore owns its complete loading lifecycle. The URL supplies identity, the data boundary verifies it, and the UI gives every outcome an intentional representation.

sections.title: A URL is an input boundary, not cached page context
sections.content: Copied links, bookmarks, refreshes, and browser restoration can enter the application at any route. A route that works only after clicking through another page is not truly addressable. Build each resource screen from URL identity plus authoritative data, with no hidden dependency on a previous component tree.

sections.title: Route parameter and resource validation
sections.content:
Parameter validation can reject impossible input before a request. For a positive numeric ID, parsing must reject empty text, non-numeric values, and values outside the allowed range. A valid-looking ID then enters the resource lookup. ‘Not found’ means that lookup has no visible record; ‘forbidden’ means the identity may exist but the caller lacks permission; ‘error’ means the lookup itself failed.

Asynchronous navigation creates a race. If the user moves from project A to project B, the A request should be aborted or its result ignored after B becomes current. Effects can use `AbortController`, while data routers can manage cancellation around route loaders. Cleanup is about correctness as well as avoiding unnecessary work.

The route should also have a recovery path: a link to the collection, a retry for transient failure, or sign-in for an authentication boundary. Links must encode resource values when constructing raw path segments. Server-side authorization is required even if the client hides unavailable links, because a person can edit the URL directly.

sections.title: A deep-linked ID passes through validation, loading, and outcome states
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[direct URL or Link] --> B[read route parameter]
  B --> C{format valid?}
  C -->|No| D[invalid-route recovery]
  C -->|Yes| E[load authorized resource]
  E --> F{outcome}
  F -->|found| G[render resource]
  F -->|missing| H[not-found screen]
  F -->|forbidden| I[access boundary]
  F -->|failed| J[retryable error]
  K[parameter changes] --> L[abort stale load]
  L --> E
```

sections.title: Load each route ID independently and cancel stale work

questions.question: Why does refreshing a React Router URL return 404, and how do you fix it?
questions.title: Fixing Refresh 404s in a BrowserRouter SPA
questions.direct_answer: Client navigation works because React Router already controls the loaded document. A refresh sends the full path, such as `/projects/atlas`, to the web server; if the server looks only for a matching file or endpoint, it returns 404 before React runs. Configure an SPA fallback to the entry document for client routes while excluding assets, APIs, and genuine server resources.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether client matching and server document delivery are understood as two layers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding only a client catch-all or rewriting assets and APIs to HTML.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe a scoped host fallback and the alternatives when it is unavailable.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Link` navigation is handled inside the already-loaded application.
Refresh and direct entry first request the current path from the server.
The host must serve the SPA entry document for valid client-side routes.
Do not rewrite assets, API endpoints, or real server files to HTML.
A client `path="*"` route cannot fix a 404 that happens before the app loads.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The 404 comes from two different navigation paths. After the SPA is loaded, a React Router `Link` updates browser history and renders a matching route inside the existing document. The web server does not need to serve a new page for that transition.

A refresh or pasted deep link is different. The browser makes a document request for the full path, for example `GET /projects/atlas`. A static server may search for a file at that location, find none, and return 404. React Router never starts because the HTML entry document was not delivered.

The usual SPA fix is a fallback or rewrite: if a request is not a real asset, API route, or server file, return `index.html` with a successful response. The application loads, reads `/projects/atlas` from browser history, and its route tree renders the correct page.

The rewrite must be scoped. Returning HTML for a missing JavaScript asset or `/api/projects` can hide deployment mistakes and break clients. The client should also have its own catch-all route for URLs that reach the app but match no valid screen; that is separate from server fallback behavior.

Hash routing avoids this hosting requirement because the fragment is not part of the server request, but it changes URLs. Server rendering or framework routing can handle real routes on the server. For a BrowserRouter SPA, a correctly scoped host fallback is the normal solution.

sections.title: The 404 happens before the client router exists
sections.content: A client route and a server resource may share the same visible path but run at different times. The server must first deliver the application shell for a valid SPA path. Only then can React Router decide which client element to render. Solving one layer does not automatically solve the other.

sections.title: Client and server not-found handling
sections.content:
The host first decides whether a request belongs to a real server concern. Static assets should return the exact asset or a real 404, and API paths should reach the API. Remaining document paths intended for the SPA can fall back to its entry HTML. Platforms express this as rewrites, fallback files, or a `try_files`-style rule, but the routing intent is the same.

After the entry document loads, React Router performs the second decision. Known paths render their route branches; an application catch-all renders a useful not-found screen for unknown client locations. This catch-all cannot influence the earlier HTTP response when the server has already rejected a direct request.

Fallback strategy depends on rendering architecture. A pure SPA uses one entry document. A pre-rendered deployment may serve generated route HTML and a separate SPA fallback. Server-rendered frameworks execute routing on the server. `HashRouter` keeps client path state after `#`, which avoids path rewrites but gives different URLs and is usually chosen only when host configuration cannot be changed.

sections.title: Client navigation and refresh meet the router at different times
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Link click] --> B[existing document]
  B --> C[React Router matches URL]
  D[refresh or pasted URL] --> E[web server receives full path]
  E --> F{asset, API, or real file?}
  F -->|Yes| G[serve that resource]
  F -->|No, valid SPA document path| H[serve app entry HTML]
  H --> C
  C --> I{client route matches?}
  I -->|Yes| J[render page]
  I -->|No| K[client not-found screen]
```

sections.title: Keep a client catch-all for unknown routes after the shell loads
